title: The Shroud of Turin: radiocarbon and later dating claims
html:
The Shroud of Turin: radiocarbon and later dating claims

1988 radiocarbon; 2022 X-ray proposal. Source record: Nature 337 (1989) 611-615; Heritage 5 (2022) 860-870.

In 1988, three laboratories (Arizona, Oxford, and the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology) dated samples from the Shroud of Turin by accelerator mass spectrometry. They reported a calibrated range of about 1260-1390 CE, published in Nature in 1989.

The sampling, the cleaning protocol, and the statistical treatment were contested at the time and remain contested by some researchers. In 2022, Liberato De Caro and colleagues published a wide-angle X-ray scattering (WAXS) study in Heritage arguing for a much earlier date, roughly the first century. The WAXS method measures cellulose ageing and depends on assumed environmental history; it has not displaced the radiocarbon result for most specialists.

Other work has examined whether the 1988 samples were contaminated by repair or by handling (Freer-Waters and Jull, npj Heritage Science, 2021 on textile fragments), and whether bleaching treatments affected the linen (Barta and Ruiz-Navas, npj Heritage Science).

What it establishes: a linen cloth of the 13th-14th century on the radiocarbon evidence, bearing an image whose formation is not fully explained. The 1988 measurement is the one result that has been independently replicated by three laboratories.

What it does not establish: any connection to Jesus. Even a first-century date, if established, would establish the age of a cloth, not its provenance or the identity of the person depicted. The dossier treats the shroud as a case study in how dating claims and their assumptions are argued, not as evidence for the resurrection.
